title: Before You Say “I Do,” Ask This One Question… It Could Save Your Marriage, Your Future, and Even Your Soul
paragraphs:
Before You Say “I Do,” Ask This One Question… It Could Save Your Marriage, Your Future, and Even Your Soul
Most people spend months preparing for a wedding. Almost no one spends enough time preparing for a covenant. One question can reveal the difference.
The room grows quiet.
The music begins.
The doors open.
Everyone stands.
Eyes fill with tears.
Phones rise into the air.
A beautiful bride walks toward the man she believes she will spend the rest of her life with.
It is one of the most breathtaking moments on earth.
But heaven is not asking whether the flowers are beautiful.
God is not measuring the elegance of the venue.
The Lord is not impressed by expensive rings, designer suits, luxury receptions, or perfectly edited wedding videos.
Before heaven witnesses your vows, there is one question that echoes through eternity.
"Is Christ truly at the center of this covenant?"
Not your feelings.
Not your chemistry.
Not your compatibility.
Not your shared hobbies.
Not even your love.
Because love alone has never been enough to sustain a covenant.
Scripture never teaches us to build marriage merely upon emotion.
It teaches us to build upon Christ.
Jesus Himself said,
"Everyone then who hears these words of Mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock." (Matthew 7:24, ESV)
Notice something remarkable.
Jesus did not say storms would avoid that house.
The storms still came.
The rain still fell.
The floods still rose.
The winds still beat against it.
The difference was not the absence of trouble.
The difference was the foundation.
That truth alone has rescued countless marriages—and exposed countless others.
Because weddings happen in a day.
Marriage happens every day afterward.
The Bible describes marriage with breathtaking depth.
In Genesis 2:24, the Hebrew says:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Al-ken ya'azov ish et-aviv ve'et-immo vedavaq be'ishto vehayu levasar echad.
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew word דָּבַק (dābaq) means far more than simply "stay together."
It carries the idea of being joined so tightly that separation becomes violent.
It is used elsewhere to describe clinging desperately, remaining inseparably attached, and pursuing covenant loyalty.
Marriage was never intended to be temporary convenience.
It was designed as covenant faithfulness.
This is why Jesus later quoted Genesis and declared,
"What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate." (Matthew 19:6)
The Greek text says:
ὃ οὖν ὁ Θεὸς συνέζευξεν
(ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen)
The verb συνέζευξεν (synezeuxen) literally means "yoked together."
It paints the picture of two lives harnessed into one purpose by God Himself.
Marriage is not merely two people agreeing to stay together.
It is God joining them together.
And if God is the One joining them, shouldn't He also be the One leading them?
That is the question so many couples forget to ask.
Because culture asks,
"Are you happy?"
God asks,
"Are you holy?"
Culture asks,
"Do they complete you?"
Christ asks,
"Will both of you become more like Me together?"
Culture celebrates attraction.
God celebrates transformation.
This is where many love stories quietly begin to unravel.
People search for "the one."
Jesus calls us to become the kind of person who faithfully loves the one He gives.
Even the Apostle Paul reveals that marriage ultimately points beyond itself.
In Ephesians 5:31–32, after quoting Genesis 2:24, he writes,
"This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church."
The Greek word for mystery is:
μυστήριον (mystērion).
Not something unknowable.
Something once hidden but now revealed by God.
Marriage is ultimately a living picture of the Gospel.
A husband sacrificially loving.
A wife responding in loving honor.
Both reflecting Christ.
Both displaying redemption.
Both reminding the world of Jesus.
That changes everything.
Suddenly marriage is no longer merely about personal fulfillment.
It becomes worship.
It becomes discipleship.
It becomes ministry.
It becomes a testimony.
And that is why one question matters above every other.
Will this marriage help both of us become more like Christ?
Not richer.
Not more comfortable.
Not more popular.
More like Jesus.
Because beauty fades.
Health changes.
Finances fluctuate.
Children grow.
Dreams evolve.
But Christ remains the same yesterday, today, and forever.
Every marriage eventually discovers what its foundation truly is.
Some discover it during financial hardship.
Some during infertility.
Some after betrayal.
Some through illness.
Some through grief.
The storm never creates the weakness.
It reveals it.
Yet here is the breathtaking hope of the Gospel.
Some marriages begin with painful scandals.
Some begin with broken histories.
Some carry shame that no one else knows.
Some couples carry addictions.
Others carry abuse.
Others carry sexual sin.
Others carry abortions.
Others carry divorce.
Others carry years of hidden guilt.
The enemy whispers,
"You'll never escape your past."
But the cross tells another story.
The Gospel has always been about God taking shattered stories and rewriting them.
King David fell.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
Rahab carried a scandalous reputation.
The Samaritan woman had five husbands.
Yet grace rewrote every one of their stories.
Not because sin was ignored.
Because repentance met mercy.
This is why our ministry exists under one unchanging message:
Not because people are good.
Because Christ is.
The Aramaic words Jesus likely spoke from the cross still echo through history:
ܐܒܐ ܫܒܘܩ ܠܗܘܢ
Abba, shboq lehon.
"Father, forgive them."
Forgiveness has always been at the center of God's story.
Marriage without forgiveness slowly dies.
Marriage with forgiveness continually reflects Christ.
Maybe you're reading this before becoming engaged.
Maybe you're already planning your wedding.
Maybe you've been married for decades.
Or maybe your marriage feels like it's hanging by a thread.
Hear this carefully.
If Jesus can redeem sinners, He can redeem marriages.
If Christ can raise the dead, He can breathe life into relationships that seem beyond repair.
But surrender must come before restoration.

The greatest wedding invitation in history is still waiting to be answered—not an invitation to an earthly ceremony, but to the eternal marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:6–9), where Christ receives His redeemed Bride. Every Christian marriage is only a shadow of that greater reality. Earthly vows point us toward the everlasting covenant secured by the blood of Jesus.
So before you ever say, "I do," ask the question that matters most:
Will saying "I do" help both of us say "Yes, Lord" every single day?
If the answer is no, pause.
If the answer is uncertain, seek wise, biblically grounded counsel.
If the answer is yes, keep Christ at the center—not only on your wedding day, but every ordinary day that follows.
Because the strongest marriages are not built by perfect people.
They are built by forgiven people who continually run back to a perfect Savior.

If this message stirred your heart, don't let it stop with you. Whether it's "Jesus, lead my future," "Pray for my marriage," or "Christ is still writing my story," your words may encourage another believer who feels alone.
Your support is more than a financial contribution—it helps proclaim the Gospel, create biblically faithful resources, and reach more hearts with the hope of Christ.
They also gain access to deeper discipleship content while helping make future Gospel-centered resources possible.
One surrendered "yes" to Jesus is infinitely greater than the most beautiful "I do" spoken without Him.
